questions.question: A constant force of $10\ \text{N}$ acts on a block that is displaced $4\ \text{m}$ along a straight line. The force makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the displacement. What is the work done by the force?

solution.key_concept: Work by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\theta$.
solution.why_not_others: $40\ \text{J}$ ignores the angle. $34.6\ \text{J}$ uses $\sin 60^\circ$ instead of $\cos 60^\circ$. Zero work requires the force to be perpendicular to the displacement.
solution.common_trap: Using $\sin\theta$ in place of $\cos\theta$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Since $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$, the answer is half of $Fd$.

questions.question: A force $F = 6x$ (in newton, with $x$ in metre) acts on a particle along the x-axis. What is the work done by this force as the particle moves from $x = 1\ \text{m}$ to $x = 3\ \text{m}$?

solution.key_concept: For a variable force, $W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$.
solution.why_not_others: $36\ \text{J}$ comes from multiplying $F(3) = 18\ \text{N}$ by the $2\ \text{m}$ displacement. $27\ \text{J}$ evaluates only the upper limit. $12\ \text{J}$ comes from $3(x_2 - x_1)^2$.
solution.common_trap: Treating a variable force as constant, i.e. writing $W = Fd$.
solution.time_saving_tip: For a linear force, use the average force: $\frac{6 + 18}{2} \times 2 = 24\ \text{J}$.

questions.question: A force acting along the x-axis on a particle varies with position as follows. It rises linearly from $0$ at $x = 0$ to $10\ \text{N}$ at $x = 4\ \text{m}$. It stays constant at $10\ \text{N}$ up to $x = 6\ \text{m}$. It then decreases linearly to $-10\ \text{N}$ at $x = 10\ \text{m}$, passing through zero at $x = 8\ \text{m}$. What is the net work done by the force from $x = 0$ to $x = 10\ \text{m}$?

solution.key_concept: Work equals the area under the F-x graph, and area below the axis counts as negative.
solution.why_not_others: $60\ \text{J}$ adds the area below the axis as positive. $50\ \text{J}$ stops the calculation at $x = 8\ \text{m}$. $20\ \text{J}$ counts only the first triangle.
solution.common_trap: Ignoring the negative sign of the area below the x-axis.
solution.time_saving_tip: The triangles from $6$ to $8\ \text{m}$ and from $8$ to $10\ \text{m}$ cancel, so only $20 + 20$ remains.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A coolie carrying a load on his head and walking on a level horizontal road does positive work on the load against gravity.
statements.R: The work done by a force is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $W = Fd\cos\theta$ is zero when $\theta = 90^\circ$.
steps: The coolie applies a vertical force on the load, while the displacement is horizontal.
With $\theta = 90^\circ$, the work done on the load is zero, so A is false.
R is a correct general statement.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Equating physical effort with work done in the physics sense.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A block of mass $m$ slides from $x = 0$ to $x = L$ on a horizontal floor where the coefficient of friction is $\mu(x) = \mu_0\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)$. The work done by friction is $-\mu_0 mgL$.
statements.II: A constant force $\vec{F} = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k})\ \text{N}$ moves a particle from the origin to the point $(1, -2, 3)\ \text{m}$. The work done by the force is $-7\ \text{J}$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Integrate a position-dependent friction force. For constant vectors, $W = F_x d_x + F_y d_y + F_z d_z$.
steps: Statement I: $W = -\int_0^L \mu_0\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right) mg\,dx = -\mu_0 mg\left(L - \frac{L}{2}\right) = -\frac{\mu_0 mgL}{2}$. So I is incorrect.
Statement II: $W = 2(1) + 3(-2) + (-1)(3) = 2 - 6 - 3 = -7\ \text{J}$. So II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I applies $W = Fd$ to a variable force, which fails. Statement II is computed correctly.
solution.common_trap: Using $\mu_0$ throughout instead of integrating $\mu(x)$.
solution.time_saving_tip: For linearly varying $\mu$, use the average value $\mu_0/2$.

questions.question: The linear momentum of a body is increased by $100\%$. What is the percentage increase in its kinetic energy?

solution.key_concept: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, so $K \propto p^2$ for a fixed mass.
solution.why_not_others: $100\%$ assumes $K \propto p$. $400\%$ confuses 'becomes 4 times' with 'increases by 400%'. $200\%$ has no physical basis here.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the final multiple with the percentage increase.

questions.question: The potential energy of a particle moving along the x-axis is $U(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - 4x$ (in joule, with $x$ in metre). At which position is the particle in stable equilibrium?

solution.key_concept: Equilibrium requires $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. It is stable if $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} > 0$.
steps: At $x = +2$ this is $4 > 0$, so the equilibrium is stable. At $x = -2$ it is negative, so that equilibrium is unstable.
solution.why_not_others: $x = -2\ \text{m}$ is a maximum of $U$, so it is unstable. At $x = 0$ the force is not zero. $x = 2\sqrt{3}\ \text{m}$ is where $U = 0$, which is not an equilibrium point.
solution.common_trap: Taking $U = 0$ as the equilibrium condition instead of $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$.

questions.question: Two bodies of masses $1\ \text{kg}$ and $4\ \text{kg}$ have equal linear momenta. What is the ratio of their kinetic energies $K_1 : K_2$?

solution.key_concept: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, so at equal momentum $K \propto \frac{1}{m}$.
solution.why_not_others: $1:4$ assumes $K \propto m$. The ratios $1:2$ and $2:1$ wrongly use $\sqrt{m}$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the heavier body must have more kinetic energy.
solution.time_saving_tip: At equal momentum, the lighter body has more kinetic energy.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Force acts along the negative x-direction

solution.key_concept: The force is $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$. A minimum of $U$ is stable, a maximum is unstable, and constant $U$ is neutral.
steps: A minimum of $U$ gives stable equilibrium: A-III.
A maximum of $U$ gives unstable equilibrium: B-IV.
If $\frac{dU}{dx} > 0$, then $F < 0$, so the force acts along $-x$: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps stable and unstable. Option (2) swaps C and D. Option (4) swaps A and C.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the minus sign in $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about kinetic and potential energy are correct?

statements.A: Kinetic energy of a body can never be negative.
statements.B: Potential energy can be negative, depending on the choice of reference level.
statements.C: A potential energy can be defined for the kinetic friction force.
statements.D: For equal momenta, the heavier body has greater kinetic energy.
statements.E: If the speed of a body is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes 9 times.

solution.key_concept: $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \ge 0$. Potential energy is defined only for conservative forces, and its reference level is arbitrary.
steps: B is true because only changes in $U$ matter, so $U$ can be negative.
C is false because friction is non-conservative.
D is false because $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, so the lighter body has more kinetic energy.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes C or D, and both are false.
solution.common_trap: Assuming potential energy exists for every force.

questions.question: A block of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ slides on a rough horizontal floor with an initial speed of $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.3$. How far does it travel before stopping? (Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.)

solution.key_concept: By the work-energy theorem, $\mu mgs = \frac{1}{2}mu^2$, so $s = \frac{u^2}{2\mu g}$.
solution.why_not_others: $12\ \text{m}$ drops the factor of 2. $3\ \text{m}$ doubles the denominator. $2\ \text{m}$ is $\frac{u}{\mu g}$, which is the stopping time in seconds, not a distance.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the mass matters. It cancels out.
solution.time_saving_tip: Stopping distance does not depend on mass for frictional retardation.

questions.question: A bullet of mass $20\ \text{g}$ moving at $300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ penetrates $0.15\ \text{m}$ into a fixed wooden block before coming to rest. What is the average resistive force exerted by the wood?

solution.key_concept: By the work-energy theorem, $Fs = \frac{1}{2}mu^2$, so $F = \frac{mu^2}{2s}$.
solution.why_not_others: $12000\ \text{N}$ omits the $\frac{1}{2}$. $3000\ \text{N}$ uses twice the penetration depth. $40\ \text{N}$ divides momentum by distance.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in kinetic energy.

questions.question: A body of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ is released from rest at a height of $5\ \text{m}$ on a rough curved track. It reaches the bottom with a speed of $8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the work done by friction? (Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.)

solution.key_concept: $W_c + W_{nc} = \Delta K$.
solution.why_not_others: $+36\ \text{J}$ has the wrong sign, since friction opposes motion. $-64\ \text{J}$ uses only the kinetic energy. $-100\ \text{J}$ uses only the gravitational work.
solution.common_trap: Giving the magnitude without the negative sign.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Two bodies of different masses with equal kinetic energies are brought to rest by equal constant retarding forces. They travel equal distances before stopping.
statements.R: The work-energy theorem is valid only for conservative forces.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $Fs = K$, so $s = \frac{K}{F}$ does not depend on mass.
steps: Equal $K$ and equal $F$ give equal $s$, so A is true.
The work-energy theorem holds for all forces, including non-conservative ones, so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1), (2) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Restricting the work-energy theorem to conservative forces.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: If the initial speed of a car is doubled and the retarding force is unchanged, its stopping distance becomes four times.
statements.II: A particle of mass $1\ \text{kg}$ starts from rest at $x = 0$ and is acted upon by a single force $F = x$ (in newton, with $x$ in metre) along the x-axis. Its speed at $x = 3\ \text{m}$ is $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $W_{net} = \Delta K$, and for a constant retarding force the stopping distance is proportional to $u^2$.
steps: Statement I: $s \propto u^2$, so doubling $u$ makes $s$ four times. I is correct.
Then $\frac{1}{2}(1)v^2 = 4.5$, so $v = 3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements check out, so options (2), (3) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Writing $W = F(3) \times 3 = 9\ \text{J}$ for a variable force.

questions.question: A motor lifts a load of $50\ \text{kg}$ vertically through $10\ \text{m}$ at a steady rate in $20\ \text{s}$. What is the power delivered by the motor? (Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.)

solution.key_concept: Power to lift a mass is $P = \frac{mgh}{t}$.
solution.why_not_others: $25\ \text{W}$ omits $g$. $5000\ \text{W}$ is the work in joules, not divided by time. $500\ \text{W}$ divides by $10\ \text{s}$ instead of $20\ \text{s}$.
solution.common_trap: Reporting the work done as the power.

questions.question: A pump ejects water at a rate of $10\ \text{kg s}^{-1}$ with a speed of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What power is required to impart this kinetic energy to the water?

solution.key_concept: $P = \frac{1}{2}\frac{dm}{dt}v^2$.
solution.why_not_others: $4\ \text{kW}$ omits the $\frac{1}{2}$. $200\ \text{W}$ uses $\frac{dm}{dt}\,v$ instead of $v^2$. $1\ \text{kW}$ introduces an extra factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ from kinetic energy.

questions.question: A body starts from rest and is driven by an engine delivering constant power. It covers a distance $s$ in time $t$. What distance does it cover, measured from the start, in time $4t$?

solution.key_concept: For constant power from rest, $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = Pt$, so $v \propto t^{1/2}$ and $s \propto t^{3/2}$.
solution.why_not_others: $16s$ assumes $s \propto t^2$, which holds for constant acceleration. $4s$ assumes $s \propto t$. $2s$ assumes $s \propto \sqrt{t}$.
solution.common_trap: Treating constant-power motion as uniformly accelerated motion.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: Power is work per unit time. The kWh is a unit of energy, and the hp is a unit of power.
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) swap the dimensions of power and work. Options (2) and (4) treat the kWh as a power.
solution.common_trap: Treating the kWh as a unit of power.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about power are correct?

statements.A: Power is a vector quantity because $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$.
statements.B: For a body starting from rest under a constant force, the instantaneous power delivered is proportional to time.
statements.C: The area under a power-time graph gives the work done.
statements.D: For a body starting from rest under constant power, its velocity is proportional to time.
statements.E: Efficiency of a machine is output power divided by input power.

solution.key_concept: Power is the scalar $\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$. For constant power from rest, $v \propto \sqrt{t}$.
steps: A is false because a dot product gives a scalar.
B is true because $v = at$, so $P = Fv = Fat \propto t$.
E is true by the definition of efficiency.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): B, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes A or D, and both are false.
solution.common_trap: Treating power as a vector because force and velocity are vectors.
